summary: All essential developer tooling and DocumentDB MCP data-plane tools are present so the Python LlamaIndex → OpenAI → Azure DocumentDB sample can be developed. However several cold-answer facts were outdated or wrong (resource types, CLI groups, auth modes, vector-search API shape, billing model and service name history) and must be corrected before code or docs are shipped. A few command-line tools (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform, dotnet) are missing but only mongosh is material to manual verification; others are optional for this sample. The build can start, but the implementer must apply the corrections below and pick concrete LLM/embedding models and index-dimension choices that the docs require for creating vector indexes.
summary_points: Data-plane tooling for Azure DocumentDB is available: the documentdb MCP server (profile "default") and multiple DocumentDB agent skills are installed; these enable inspecting collections, creating indexes and running queries.

Multiple cold answers were incorrect/outdated: the correct ARM/CLI resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and the CLI group is az documentdb (extension), not az cosmosdb/databaseAccounts.
Azure DocumentDB uses vCore compute tiers (M30 etc.) and has a vCore + storage pricing model (not RU/s). This matters for provisioning and examples.
Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) is supported for data-plane access (mongodb+srv with MONGODB-OIDC); SCRAM is still supported. The sample should support both and document how to enable Entra auth.

Vector search uses DocumentDB-specific 'cosmosSearch' indexes (kinds: vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, vector-diskann) and $search with the cosmosSearch operator — do not reuse Atlas/driver-specific vector syntax.
Missing CLI tools: mongosh is the only blocker for convenient manual verification; azd/bicep/terraform/dotnet are optional for this sample and can be deferred.

tools.name: python
tools.needed_for: Run the sample app, create the virtualenv, install dependencies, run seed scripts and tests.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or test the Python LlamaIndex pipeline locally.
tools.workaround: Install Python 3.10+; the sample target is Python 3.10+ but 3.11+ is acceptable. Use a container if local Python cannot be installed.

tools.name: pip
tools.needed_for: Install Python dependencies (pymongo, llama-index, openai client or equivalent).
tools.detail: pip available via virtualenv per run environment note
tools.workaround: Use pip bundled in the Python distribution or use a requirements-based Docker image.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure subscriptions and optionally run ARM/Bicep/Terraform deploys or retrieve management-plane info; also to install/upgrade the documentdb az extension if needed.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot manage Azure resources or run CLI quickstart steps; some diagnostics or firewall rule edits would be harder.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal for management tasks or run required ARM calls via REST, but az is strongly recommended.

tools.name: node / npx
tools.needed_for: Run/boot MCP servers (npx github:microsoft/documentdb-mcp) for agent tooling and to install agent skills if needed.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run the documentdb MCP server locally via npx; MCP-based inspection tooling would be harder to wire up.
tools.workaround: Use a preinstalled MCP server binary if available or use the Azure portal / Azure SDK for management tasks.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional: run a local DocumentDB gateway for development and tests (gateway image exposes Mongo gateway on port 10260).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run a local documentdb gateway container; will need to test against the live cluster.
tools.workaround: Test against the provided live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) or use a hosted dev cluster.

tools.name: git
tools.needed_for: Source control for the sample repo and to clone upstream installer/agent kit repos if needed.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot clone or publish code; slows iterative development.
tools.workaround: Download zip from GitHub when necessary.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane inspection and management: listing databases/collections, sampling documents, creating/checking indexes, running explain(), and inserting sample data during build verification.
tools.detail: MCP server 'documentdb' present with 18 data-plane tools (list_databases, find_documents, insert_documents, create_index, list_indexes, explain_operation, etc.) (inventory)
tools.impact_if_missing: Agent cannot inspect or verify the live cluster programmatically; manual portal checks would be required.
tools.workaround: Use Azure portal and SDKs (pymongo) to inspect the cluster, or install the documentdb MCP server via npx as described in the documentdb-mcp-setup skill.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn docs search)
tools.needed_for: Grounding facts and examples in up-to-date Microsoft documentation about resource types, CLI commands, vector search syntax, authentication and more.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to verify current best-practice pages and quickstarts programmatically.
tools.workaround: Search docs manually in the browser; ensure pages used are the current Learn pages.

tools.name: documentdb-driver (skill)
tools.needed_for: Driver usage and patterns: recommended client (pymongo), singleton MongoClient patterns, timeouts, pooling for Azure DocumentDB.
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of misinitializing clients (pool exhaustion, improper timeouts) and shipping anti-patterns.
tools.workaround: Follow standard pymongo docs, but the skill contains DocumentDB-specific guidance.

tools.name: documentdb-connection (skill)
tools.needed_for: Connection tuning for MongoClient, pool sizes and timeouts appropriate for serverless vs OLTP; helpful for serverless / function examples.
tools.impact_if_missing: Less specific guidance on connection-pool tuning and transient error handling.
tools.workaround: Use generic pymongo connection settings and increase timeouts conservatively.

tools.name: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: Local development guidance and Docker gateway details (port 10260), TLS config and env-driven config.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to set up a local dev gateway with correct ports/TLS options.
tools.workaround: Follow Learn quickstarts or run a local MongoDB server, but feature parity may differ.

tools.name: documentdb-vector-search (skill)
tools.needed_for: Guidance on which vector index kinds to pick (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF), index options, and $search/cosmosSearch usage for hybrid queries.
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of creating an incompatible vector index shape or misconfiguring dimensions/algorithms.
tools.workaround: Follow Learn vector-search docs; pick DiskANN for M30+ and choose embedding dimensionality to match the chosen model.

tools.name: documentdb-indexing (skill)
tools.needed_for: Advice on single-field, compound and vector indexes, and how to design indexes for queries the sample will run (lookup by patientId, vector search on embedding field).
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of poor query performance and accidentally creating expensive indexes.
tools.workaround: Follow Learn indexing docs and the skill's cookbook when designing indexes.

tools.name: documentdb-data-modeling (skill)
tools.needed_for: Schema recommendations (embedding vs referencing), adding schemaVersion and createdAt fields, 16 MB limits, and sample collection shape.
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of producing documents that hit the size limit or poor query shapes.
tools.workaround: Use standard denormalization patterns and schemaVersion field; keep documents small.

tools.name: documentdb-mcp-setup (skill)
tools.needed_for: How to wire the DocumentDB MCP server into agentic clients and how CONNECTION_PROFILES should be configured (safety rules about secrets).
tools.impact_if_missing: Agent can't advise or configure MCP clients safely.
tools.workaround: Manually configure CONNECTION_PROFILES and follow the skill's listed security rules.

tools.name: documentdb-security (skill)
tools.needed_for: Security guidance: TLS, Private Endpoint, Microsoft Entra ID setup, RBAC, and CMK guidance for sample README notes.
tools.impact_if_missing: Sample README could omit critical security caveats for PHI handling and Entra setup.
tools.workaround: Refer to Learn security docs; include a strong warning about not using real PHI in the sample.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type (account-level): Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (eg. Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/my-documentdb-account).
confusions.grounded_answer: The current resource type for managed Azure DocumentDB clusters is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource provider Microsoft.DocumentDB).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB docs and older ARM templates historically exposed Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB accounts; the new dedicated vCore-managed Mongo clusters use the mongoClusters resource type.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts in Bicep/ARM or az cosmosdb commands would target the wrong control-plane resource and could fail or create a different service (Cosmos DB account). The sample's IaC or CLI steps would be incorrect.
improvements: Update any quickstart or README that mentions Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts to reference Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters when describing vCore DocumentDB clusters (Learn 'mongoClusters' page).
Add a deprecation note on older 'databaseAccounts' template pages for Mongo/vCore scenarios to point to the new 'mongoClusters' resource type.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core 'az cosmosdb' CLI group. To create a Mongo-compatible account: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRG --locations regionName=westus --kind MongoDB (or --capabilities EnableMongo).
confusions.grounded_answer: The management CLI for the vCore-managed DocumentDB clusters is 'az documentdb' (documentdb extension/commands), e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster show. There is also an az extension named 'documentdb' used by the CLI docs.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB 'az cosmosdb' command group manages Cosmos DB databaseAccounts. The new vCore DocumentDB clusters have their own CLI commands under az documentdb (documentdb extension).

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb CLI group (older Cosmos docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands to manage a mongoClusters resource will either fail or operate against the wrong service; scripts and docs calling the wrong CLI group will not work for vCore clusters.
improvements: Change sample README/Quickstart to use az documentdb mongocluster commands and include the note to install/upgrade the 'documentdb' az extension when necessary (Learn quickstart).
Add an explicit comment in agent guidance that 'az cosmosdb' is for Cosmos accounts and 'az documentdb' manages vCore mongoClusters.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep/ARM resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform resource: azurerm_cosmosdb_account.
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore DocumentDB clusters the ARM/Bicep resource is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; Terraform should use the corresponding AzAPI / provider resource (or azurerm provider module that wraps mongoClusters). The older azurerm_cosmosdb_account/ Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts resource is for Cosmos DB account-style resources, not the vCore mongoClusters resource.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically Cosmos DB used Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts and azurerm_cosmosdb_account; the vCore-managed Mongo offering uses a separate resource type (mongoClusters) that the cold answer did not reflect.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong ARM/Terraform resource type would attempt to create/modify different control-plane resources, leading to provisioning failures or the wrong infrastructure.
improvements: Update any Bicep/Terraform sample templates to use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and include a small Bicep example in the README.
Add a one-line note in the agent kit making explicit which ARM/Terraform resource to use for vCore clusters vs Cosmos RU accounts.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB-style URI. Example: mongodb://<username>:<password>@myaccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Host suffix typically: .mongo.cosmos.azure.com (account.mongo.cosmos.azure.com). Port: 10255 for TLS. Required options: ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false; username often in the form "<dbuser>@<account>" when using Cosmos Mongo API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters use Mongo-style URIs but with the mongoClusters host suffix and new SRV patterns. Example documented connection strings use mongodb+srv:// or mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster-name>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com for Entra OIDC, and the management tools return connection strings. TLS must be enabled (tls=true/tls in modern clients). Do not assume the older cosmos 'mongo.cosmos.azure.com' host or port 10255; DocumentDB exposes SRV endpoints like '<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com' and the CLI/sdk provides connection-string retrieval commands.

grounding_links.title: Get connection strings for a mongo cluster (examples)
Get-AzDocumentDBMongoClusterConnectionString (PowerShell docs showing mongodb+srv)
Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflects the older Cosmos DB Mongo endpoint hostnames and port (10255) used by some Cosmos DB accounts; vCore DocumentDB clusters use different SRV-hosted endpoints and may present mongodb+srv URIs and different host suffixes.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo connection string docs (example)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix/port or options will cause client connection failures; the sample must request the exact connection string from the portal or the az documentdb CLI and read it from env (DOCUMENTDB_URI).
improvements: In the sample README, replace any example connection string that uses .mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 with instructions to retrieve the cluster's connection string (az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings or portal) and to read it from DOCUMENTDB_URI.
Add an explicit note in the MCP setup skill docs that the MCP profile should use the cluster's provided connection string and that TLS must be present.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed in Request Units (RUs) for Cosmos DB API: you provision RU/s at database or container level or use autoscale; Cosmos also offers a serverless option for some scenarios. There is not a vCore-based billing model for the Cosmos DB Mongo-compatible API (classic model is RU-based).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters are billed by compute tier (vCore-based tiers like M30, M40, etc.) plus storage; they are not the RU/s Cosmos billing model. The vCore model is the intended pricing for DocumentDB vCore clusters (sample run environment uses M30).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI (references to tiers M30/M40)
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (pricing and vCore references)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes Cosmos DB's RU model (used by Cosmos DB 'for NoSQL' and older Cosmos Mongo API RU-mode). The vCore-based DocumentDB clusters use compute tiers (M-series) and storage pricing.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB RU model docs (older Cosmos RU docs)

confusions.build_risk: If the sample assumes RU/s for provisioning guidance, example cost estimates and sample CLI flags will be wrong; using a wrong capacity model could lead to wrong recommendations and confusing sample defaults.
improvements: Update README and any provisioning snippets to explain the vCore + storage pricing model for DocumentDB clusters and mention that RUs are a different Cosmos model.
If the repo contains optional IaC, include both a vCore (mongoClusters) example and a brief note directing readers to the RU-based Cosmos offering if they need RU semantics.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Data-plane authentication for the MongoDB API is via database users / SCRAM (username/password created in the account) in the MongoDB connection string. Management/ARM operations use Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) RBAC. Direct MongoDB driver authentication using Azure AD tokens is not generally supported for the Mongo API; use the SCRAM credentials in the connection URI. For management operations use az login / service principal and Azure AD tokens.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both Native (SCRAM) database users and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) data-plane authentication. Entra authentication is available when enabled on the cluster; the client connection string uses authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC / MONGODB-OIDC or MONGODB-OIDC properties (examples use mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC&authMechanismProperties=ENVIRONMENT:azure,TOKEN_RESOURCE:...). Drivers and tools (MongoDB Compass, mongosh with OIDC support) can authenticate via managed identities or interactive sign-in; cluster config must allow MicrosoftEntraID in authConfig.allowedModes.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (how-to)
Enable Microsoft Entra ID authentication (CLI example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described older Cosmos Mongo offerings where only SCRAM database users were commonly documented; modern DocumentDB vCore clusters added OIDC/Entra support and explicit cluster flags to enable MicrosoftEntraID mode.

confusion_sources.title: Docs that appear to only show SCRAM examples (older quickstarts)

confusions.build_risk: If the sample assumes only SCRAM authentication, it misses an important modern option (managed identity / OIDC) that many enterprise customers will prefer. The sample should document both methods and how to enable Entra auth on the cluster.
improvements: Add a short 'Authentication' section to the README showing both SCRAM (connection string via DOCUMENTDB_URI) and Microsoft Entra ID (example mongodb+srv with MONGODB-OIDC, and steps to register a managed identity) with Learn links.
In the MCP setup guidance, document how to register managed identities and enable MicrosoftEntraID in the cluster's authConfig (link to the CLI and portal steps).

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB-compatible endpoint use the standard MongoDB drivers. For Python use pymongo or motor (async). There is also the Azure SDK (azure-cosmos) but for Mongo wire-protocol access you should use official MongoDB drivers rather than a Cosmos-specific SDK.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the standard MongoDB drivers (PyMongo for Python, motor for async). For vCore DocumentDB clusters you should use standard MongoDB drivers and tools (mongosh, Compass) — there isn't a separate DocumentDB-specific Python driver for the Mongo wire protocol.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Mongoose to Azure DocumentDB (driver example)
What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None if PyMongo is used; using azure-cosmos instead would be incorrect for Mongo wire-protocol operations.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: On a MongoDB-style cluster the common vector index type is HNSW. Create with a MongoDB createIndex call on the vector field; example (pseudocode): db.summaries.createIndex( { embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'embed_idx', indexType: 'HNSW', metric: 'cosine', dimensions: 1536 } ). (Exact option names vary by implementation; the general form is db.COL.createIndex({vectorField:'vector'}, {indexType:'HNSW', metric:'cosine', ...}).)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector index kinds vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, and vector-diskann with provider-specific options. You create them with a createIndexes-style command that uses a 'cosmosSearch' / 'cosmosSearchOptions' block, e.g. a JSON createIndexes/createSearchIndexes payload specifying kind: 'vector-hnsw' or 'vector-diskann' plus algorithm parameters (m, efConstruction, dimensions, similarity). Querying uses the $search stage with the cosmosSearch operator.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-hnsw / vector-ivf / vector-diskann examples)
Create a DiskANN index and DiskANN options

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a generic MongoDB createIndex shape and Atlas-like vector index options; DocumentDB requires its cosmosSearchOptions shape and specific 'kind' strings (vector-hnsw, vector-ivf, vector-diskann).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder issues a generic createIndex call using Atlas syntax, index creation will fail and vector search won't work; the sample must call the DocumentDB create-index API with cosmosSearchOptions or use the appropriate driver call that wraps it.
improvements: In the sample's index creation helper, include the exact JSON body used by DocumentDB (cosmosSearchOptions with kind and parameter names) and a comment linking to the Learn vector-search docs.
Add a small helper function in the repo to create a DiskANN/HNSW/IVF index with the correct options and check for existence before creating it.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Basic full-text search uses MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({field:'text'})) and $text queries. For hybrid vector+text search you typically combine a vector index (as above) with text indexing in the application or use an external search service (Azure Cognitive Search) or a specialized search engine. There is no single built-in hybrid search API in the classic Cosmos Mongo API; you combine vector and text queries at the application level or use an external search product.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides integrated full-text and vector search and a hybrid search capability via the new $search aggregation stage with the cosmosSearch operator; full-text and vector features are integrated (cosmosSearch supports lexical and vector criteria together). You should use the DocumentDB createSearchIndexes/cosmosSearch syntax and $search/cosmosSearch operator for hybrid queries rather than stitching two independent queries client-side.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB and $search / cosmosSearch operator
Full-text and hybrid search guidance

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described the classic MongoDB $text approach and mixing vector search externally; DocumentDB provides integrated hybrid search and a dedicated operator (cosmosSearch) for combining text + vector semantics.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample uses client-side hybrid logic instead of cosmosSearch, it will be less efficient, may return inconsistent ranking, and will miss functionality (searchScore metadata and server-side filtering).
improvements: Use the cosmosSearch operator in sample queries for hybrid retrieval and show an example aggregation pipeline in the README.
Document that createSearchIndexes / cosmosSearchOptions must be used to provision indexes used by $search queries.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB's MongoDB API historically supports a subset of MongoDB server versions (various accounts support 3.6, 4.0, 4.2, 5.0 and more recently 6.0 for supported wire protocol). Not all MongoDB features are supported: server-side JavaScript ($where), some admin commands, certain aggregation stages and change stream semantics can differ or be unavailable. Expect differences in transactions, TTL, and some operators depending on the account's API-version/compatibility.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (per the compatibility docs) and advertises ~99% operator compatibility; some MongoDB admin or server-only commands and certain operators remain unsupported (see the MQL compatibility docs for the exact operator matrix). DocumentDB supports multi-document transactions, most aggregation stages, and documents explicit compatibility tables per server-version.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB (supported versions and operators)
Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas (wire protocol versions)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer gave an older list and was vague; the product now documents explicit wire-protocol support up to newer versions (5.0–8.0) and an operator compatibility matrix.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming unsupported operators or older server versions will cause runtime failures during migration; the sample should run its queries against the target cluster and include compatibility checks if relying on advanced aggregation stages.
improvements: Add a short 'Compatibility' section to the sample README that points to the MQL compatibility table and recommends testing any unusual aggregation stages against the target cluster.
When the sample constructs test queries, include a step that runs explain('executionStats') via the documentdb MCP explain tool to verify index usage and compatibility.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is a Cosmos DB emulator but it only supports the SQL API; it does not emulate the MongoDB wire protocol reliably. For MongoDB API development run a local MongoDB server (official image) matching the wire version you need, e.g. docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo -d mongo:6.0. Connect on port 27017 for local testing with standard MongoDB drivers.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a local DocumentDB gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes a MongoDB-wire-compatible gateway on port 10260. The Learn docs and local-deployment guidance recommend using the DocumentDB gateway image (port 10260) for local dev to match service behavior (TLS, SCRAM, and DocumentDB features).

grounding_links.title: Run DocumentDB locally - gateway Docker image and port 10260
documentdb-local-deployment

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer suggested using plain MongoDB for local dev; while that is sometimes acceptable, DocumentDB provides a local gateway image that better matches production (port 10260) and should be used for parity testing.
confusions.build_risk: Using plain MongoDB locally may hide compatibility issues (vector index features, Entra OIDC support, DocumentDB-specific query nuances). The sample should prefer the DocumentDB gateway for integration tests.
improvements: Document the recommended local dev image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) and the port 10260 in the README and in the sample's local-dev instructions.
Add a docker-compose file in the repo that starts the gateway on 127.0.0.1:10260 (with SKIP_INIT_DATA option available).

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Support for MongoDB change streams depends on the MongoDB wire-version compatibility of the account. Some Cosmos/Mongo-compatible accounts historically did not support change streams, or supported a limited form. If change streams are supported they usually require the account to advertise a replica-set-like topology (handled by the service) and the driver to use watch(). Expect to verify support for change streams on your specific account before relying on them.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports change streams; there is a documented 'Change streams' feature with specific guidance. For some multishard scenarios or for historical limitations you may need to enable a preview feature or rebalancer settings in the portal (the docs explain enabling change streams for multishard clusters). Use the change-stream docs and follow the enablement steps for preview features if required.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB
Mongoose tutorial notes mentioning Model.watch() and change-stream preview enabling

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer hedged because change stream semantics and availability historically varied between services; DocumentDB now documents change streams and the enablement steps for particular cluster/topologies.
confusions.build_risk: If the sample tries to use change streams without verifying the target cluster's configuration (preview feature or multishard enablement), watch() calls may fail. The build must include a check or a README note explaining how to enable change streams for the cluster used in tests.
improvements: Add a small section in the README that explains how to verify change-stream support and how to enable the preview feature for multishard clusters if needed (link to change-streams docs).
When writing unit/integration tests that rely on change streams, include a guard that checks the cluster's change-stream capability and skips tests when unavailable.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the service-specific MCP server named 'documentdb' for data-plane inspection and tooling; the general azure MCP server does not provide the same documentdb-specific inspection/agent tools. The sample environment expects the 'documentdb' MCP server with a connection profile named 'default'.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides rich data-plane tools (list_databases, find_documents, create_index, explain_operation, etc.) and is the right tool for programmatic inspection and verification; the general azure MCP server is separate and does not replace documentdb data-plane tools.

grounding_links.title: documentdb (MCP server) - inventory entry

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: n/a
confusions.build_risk: None; the inventory confirms the documentdb MCP server is available and should be used for all data-plane checks.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name for Microsoft's multi-model, globally distributed database service; it was later rebranded/expanded as Azure Cosmos DB. The Azure 'DocumentDB' name historically refers to that service (not the separate open-source DocumentDB project). The MongoDB-compatible offering is an API surface on top of the Cosmos engine (or the managed DocumentDB service) that speaks the MongoDB wire protocol but is backed by Microsoft's platform.
confusions.grounded_answer: The current 'Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)' name was previously the vCore-based 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' — it was renamed to Azure DocumentDB to align with the open-source DocumentDB engine that powers it. Note: there is historical ambiguity because 'Azure DocumentDB' was the original name of the service that later became Cosmos DB in 2017; the new name reuses 'DocumentDB' but refers to the vCore Mongo offering built on the open-source DocumentDB engine.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)? (naming and history)
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (naming notes)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Product names have changed over time and the same term 'DocumentDB' was used in different eras; the cold answer conflated the earlier 2014 DocumentDB → Cosmos rename with the later vCore 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' → 'Azure DocumentDB' rename.
confusions.build_risk: Naming confusion in docs or READMEs could lead builders to pick the wrong CLI commands, ARM resource types, or billing model. Clear naming in the sample is required.
improvements: In the sample README, include a short 'Naming' note: list the previous names and explicitly map which API/resource/CLI to use (vCore clusters -> Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters -> az documentdb).
Where older docs are linked, add a one-line disclaimer that the page may refer to databaseAccounts and RU-mode Cosmos offerings and provide the correct link to mongoClusters.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The underlying engine is the service's proprietary Cosmos/DocumentDB engine (a MongoDB-wire-protocol translation layer), not a stock MongoDB server. For applications this means you should use standard MongoDB drivers and expect most queries and CRUD to work the same, but some server-specific features, admin commands, and edge behaviors (transactions, change streams, certain aggregation stages) may differ; test critical functionality against the target account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is powered by the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project) built on PostgreSQL and exposes the MongoDB wire protocol. Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers, but must be aware of documented compatibility differences; the open-source engine means the same engine can be run locally or self-hosted.

confusions.question: How should the sample obtain the cluster connection string at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the MongoDB-style connection URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to pymongo.MongoClient. Example in Python: client = pymongo.MongoClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']). Do not hard-code the URI or write it to logs.

confusions.question: What document schema and collection will the sample create to store session summaries?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a collection named 'summaries' in database 'sample_healthcare_14'. Each document: { patientId: '<patient-id>', sessionId: '<session-id>', createdAt: ISODate(...), chief_complaint: '...', assessment: '...', plan: '...', follow_up: '...', embedding: [float,...] (optional), sourceTranscriptId: '<id>' }. Index on { patientId: 1, sessionId: 1 } and a vector index on 'embedding' if the cluster supports vector indexes.
confusions.grounded_answer: This schema is appropriate and aligns with documentdb-data-modeling and vector-search guidance: use a 'summaries' (or 'clinical_summaries') collection with fields patientId, sessionId, createdAt, chief_complaint, assessment, plan, follow_up, optional embedding array, and an index on patientId/sessionId plus a vector index on the embedding path created via cosmosSearchOptions when embeddings are used.
